title: Building a Sanctuary, Coming Home to Continuous Practice
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose closes an eight-week study of Shitou's Song of the Grass Roof Hermitage by taking up Case 4 of the Book of Serenity, in which Indra plants a blade of grass and declares the sanctuary built. Joden pairs the koan with Manjushri asking Sudhana for one stalk of medicinal herb, and with the Zoom sangha, where pandemic limits turn scattered homes into knots in Indra's net. Dogen on practice without a monk's hall and Suzuki Roshi's sixteen-foot golden Buddha made from one blade of grass show how little a sanctuary needs. Joden recalls sitting on the edge of a bed in Barcelona, in the fo'c'sle of a purse seiner, and facing a stucco wall in Mexico.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
[unclear: "Cannot be heard."] Good morning, friends and fellow bodhisattvas.
This morning I've entitled my talk "Building a Sanctuary: Coming Home to Continuous Practice."
At the last class we asked each of you to come up with a line that you had focused on, and I didn't do that, because I've been focusing on the whole poem, throughout the whole poem.
Then as I put this talk together, I realized that the line I was going to focus on is firmly based on steadiness.
It can't be surpassed.

So I come to you today with a great humility of how little I understand, and a sense that, as Nina and Susan Elby said at last Sunday's services, I have cobbled together some remarks that I trust will approach some sense.
There is certainly no final answer or definitive statement.
Perhaps I will strike the right strings in the right order and produce some harmonious sounds.
After each Grass Hut class I have had Dokusan with Nomon Tim.

A few weeks back I told him that in considering my investigations for each class, I felt like I had walked on a beach and picked up some cool Dharma rocks, Susan's cobbles, and come home and put together a collage.
Did I pick out the right rocks for the moment?

Each time I started to prepare by opening a text, it felt like my instinctive response was to read one line, be reminded of a reference or read a footnote, and suddenly I'm off down another rabbit hole, down a tunnel.
Do I go down one of Alice's rabbit holes, a passage to another dimension?
Or is it a shortcut, or the roundabout way to exactly where I need to find?
How many other texts could I have chosen?
Were there too many?
Tomorrow, next second, I'd make different choices.
And in a startled moment I realized the second Dharma name Nomon Tim wrote on my rakusu was Kyoto, studying the way.
Is this my way of meeting the ancestral teachers and becoming familiar with their instructions?
Kyoto, by the way, in Japanese phonics also means archer.
So I wonder, with all these texts, am I trying too hard to hit the supposed bullseye?
Or am I like the Zen master with an expectant audience at Esalen that Jeff Bickner told us about a few Sundays ago?
Do I aim for the target and then pivot and shoot the arrow out to the open Pacific?

In his final chapter, Ben Connolly reminds us that the poem holds forth the grand possibility of seeing how our small immediate moment-to-moment human effort is connected to the incredible vastness of everything, of everyone.

The poem encourages us to see that the way to realize this possibility of connectedness, of making real the promise of having our selfless lives as a contribution to the wellness of all things, is to simply bring our whole selves in this body to this place and this moment, here and now.
Don't separate from this skin bag.

As some of you noted in our final class the other night, Connolly stresses relax and ease, a great relief to those of us who find ourselves perhaps striving and stressing to reach some imagined goal of understanding or realization.
And just as I was sitting before this talk, I realized that there's this great tension in this poem between don't give up and letting go, holding on and letting go, staying steady and letting go.

So this talk is really on a theme of emphasizing steadiness of regular and continuous practice, to our devotion as individuals and as the sangha, our commitment to exploring each moment, this moment in this body and in this place we are so fortunate to inhabit.
Each of us cobbles together a sanctuary with little pretense, a figurative grass hut, a perishable corner, a location.
What matters is our intention, our devotion to practice and to the precepts, our efforts to live an upright life rather than an uptight life.
But it's a pattern, a set of habits we are not so attached to that if circumstances don't allow our accustomed situation of time and space, you can still carry on.
We each do the best we can with what we have, where we are, and try not to get caught in the illusion that the setup isn't right enough or good enough to allow us to sit calmly with head covered.
Each moment offers the opportunity to fully enter this perishable place of continuing delusion and enlightenment.
Or as one of you said during Wednesday's discussion, the possibility of polishing the moment.
That phrase reminded me of Suzuki Roshi's endearing "you are perfect exactly the way you are, but there's always room for improvement."
Or the old Boy Scout notion of leaving a place better than you found it.
Every moment is an opportunity to practice compassion, compassion, generosity, and joy, continuing practice.
We have spent the last eight weeks reading Sherdoo's Song of the Grass Roof Hermitage, a kind of guide for realizing and finding our place for practice and meditation.
How do we each create our own place and occupy and use our time after we rise from the cushion, to comport ourselves in the great vehicle of Bodhisattva way?
We began our investigation of this nearly forgotten text by considering Sherdoo's situation in the middle of the An Lushan Rebellion after years of devastating war.
Yet he found a place of refuge on a flat rock and a practice of steadiness.

And we have each considered and responded to our own situation of suffering through the past years of Trump, George Floyd's public murder, the Black Lives Matter movement, a nail-biting election followed by fraud, chicanery, and the horror of an armed insurrection fomented by our own president.
And that list doesn't include the COVID epidemic, pandemic, a public health catastrophe, the likes of which none of us have ever lived through.
There is no comparison comparing our catastrophes to those of Sherdoo's eighth century China.
When Du Fu wrote, *heaven and earth are racked with ruin, sorrow and sorrow no end in sight.* But clearly our optimistic American expectations of stability and order have been severely disrupted.
COVID has forced us to radically change all aspects of our social and business lives, transformed how we practice with each other on a day-to-day basis.
But it has also provided us an interesting view of how we view of how we respond as individual bodhisattvas and as a sangha.

This viral catastrophe, a character in Chinese also translated as opportunity, has raised profound questions about how we go forward in the middle of our tragic and joyous world, a world in which we are continuously reminded by internet and television how deeply and extensively our planet and our fellow beings, sentient and non-sentient, suffer.
A year ago, just as we were about to renew our lease on the Forest Street Zendo, we realized it could be a year or longer before we could gather together in that space.
So we jumped the 100-foot pole and entered this Zoom universe, not really understanding where or how we would land.
And here we are today.
What have we realized in this transformation of our practice?
Ryushin Philip Whelan, great poet and Buddhist teacher of whom [unclear: "Zucchetto"] is his literary executor, was fond of composer Igor Stravinsky's notion that limits make us more creative.
So here's a quote from Igor Stravinsky.
*So here we are, whether we like it or not, in the realm of necessity.
Well, in art, as in everything else, one can build only upon a resisting foundation.
Whatever constantly gives way to pressure constantly renders movement impossible.
My freedom will be so much the greater and more meaningful the more narrowly I limit my field of action and the more I surround myself with obstacles.
Whatever diminishes constraint diminishes strength.
The more constraints one imposes, the more frees oneself of the chains that shackle the spirit.*
Others more recently have called this creative limitation, or the concept of how purposefully limiting oneself can actually drive creativity.
As artist Phil Hanson stated in a TED talk, we need to first be limited in order to become limitless.
And if you treat the problems as possibilities, life will start to dance with you in the most amazing ways.
So how are we taken, and how do we continue to take this period of limitation, the constraint of not being able to physically gather together, and turn it into an opportunity for limitlessness?
And even as we can see the horizon of these limits coming to an end, how do we retain the habits and patterns we have embodied to further our exploration of the Buddha way?
At the core of our practice is zazen.
We can practice alone, at regular services, or as we are doing now, for extended periods such as during a sesshin.

One of our teachers said that given a choice of how and when we enter the time and space when all things are at rest, if there's a choice between attending a sesshin, participating in weekly services or having a regular daily practice, the choice should be daily practice.
Yes, a sesshin such as this one offers an intense experience.
You can even have a beneficial hangover for a few days.
And weekly practice is really encouraging, and services remind us of the ritual framework of our tradition.
But the days in between allow a kind of [unclear: "attention strain"].
Daily practice blesses us with a regularity that we begin to miss if circumstances prevent our settling down and re-engaging with that calm center of our lives.
It becomes a healthy habit for mind and body, kind of like brushing your teeth.
Zoom has been a revelation, especially to those of us who are technologically averse.
Many of us had already had a morning sitting practice by ourselves, something we had to do, responding to the sound of the bell.

Zoom has provided a regularly available time and virtual space to be together, encouraging our regular and mutual practice as a sangha in a way we wouldn't have considered if we had to drive to the dharma hall from all over the region.
But it also reveals some of the intimate details of how and where each of us sit, a peek into each of our homes.
You've all seen the duck decoys on top of my bookcase, Edie's shoji screen, the altar in Kate's basement, and Tim's guitars hanging on the wall.
In a curious inversion, Zoom has made sangha more real, intimate, and stable on a daily basis, even though it truly is a virtual reality, a kind of hologram, an illusion of electrons.

But in the absence of being able to chant and sit together in real time and physical space, we have not only accepted this limitation, we have created a kind of limitlessness that few of us could have predicted or anticipated.

Shurju's direction to buy grasses to build a hut and don't give up is to build a refuge we know is safe in this world, yet temporary and also necessary, all-inclusive and uniquely our own, reflective of the universe and absent of any enduring identity.
In Zen, there is an expression of being a person of no status, and a self-declaration: I am that man, or I am that woman.
We are each a unique, self-contained, open-hearted, receptive, present, and empty, interpenetrated skin bag.
So what are these grasses that Shurju urges us to bind together?

And how does our understanding encourage our practice in our own huts, scattered across the Zoom Dharma Mountain from Bellingham to British Columbia, from Anacortes to California, the vast spaces of Arizona, Colorado, and Saskatchewan?
The reaches of the vast and wide universe are present for us all on a screen.
How curious, how wonderful, how incomprehensible when you start thinking about how this can all happen.
Yet it does, and so it is.
The Ancestral Teachers provide three instructive stories about how to look at the grasses we bind together to build our practice reality.
In our teachings, we know grass is a shorthand for the phenomenal world.

And in our experience, we know grasses can range from what we call a weed, which is really just a name for a grass we haven't found a use for, and whether that weed is marijuana or dandelion or reed canary grass, or it's bamboo, wheat, millet, corn, a tall eucalyptus or an ancient redwood or an elephant or the person sitting next to us in real or cyberspace.
Layman Pang says the thousand grass tips are the minds of the ancestors.
Dogen and Uji, his fascicle on the nature of time, tells us:
*Know that in this way there are a myriad of forms and hundreds of grasses, all things, throughout the entire earth, and yet each grass and each form itself is the entire earth.
The study of this is the beginning of practice.*
Let me read that again.
*Know that in this way there are myriads of forms and hundreds of grasses, all things, throughout the entire earth, and yet each grass and each*
form itself is the entire earth.
The study of this is the beginning of practice.
Each thing, each grass, each form can be, must be studied, or as Dogen would say, investigated as we step into our practice, as we live our lives.
And as we know, the grasses keep emerging, so our investigations continue on and on.
There is a story Dogen offers about the nature of grass in his Eihei Koroku.

Sudhana, the hero of the Flower Ornament Sutra, a favorite of [unclear: "Shuddho Krish's"] and the [unclear: "cortex for Huayang"] Buddhist teachings, studied with Manjushri, the Bodhisattva of wisdom.
Manjushri asked Sudhana to go out and bring him back one stalk of medicinal herb.
Sudhana leaves, looks throughout the entire earth, but finds nothing that is not medicine.
He comes back to Manjushri and says, "The entire great earth is medicine.
Which one should I bring you?"
Manjushri says, "Bring back one stalk of medicinal herb."
Sudhana plucked one blade of grass and gave it to Manjushri.
Manjushri held up the single blade, showed it to the assembly, and said, "This one blade of grass both can kill a person and can give them life."
The awesome power of a blade of grass: life and death, depending on how it is used and who uses it.
Manjushri's sword giving wisdom, demolishing delusion.
The healing power, the destructive power.
How do we use what is in front of us appropriately just then?
How do we respond to what [unclear: "Shuddhu says meets the eye"]?
Which grasses, which elements of the great earth do we choose to build our lives, our practice?
Another grass story is in Koan 4 in the Book of Serenity that speaks also of how we find the materials that we use to establish our hut, our practice space.
It begins with an introduction.
*As soon as a single dust mote arises, the whole earth is contained therein.
With a single horse and a single lance, the empire is extended.
Who is this person who can be master in any place and meet the source in everything?*
And the case reads this way.
*As the world-honored one was walking with the congregation, he pointed to the ground with his finger and said, "This spot is good to build a sanctuary."
Indra, the emperor of the gods, took a blade of grass, stuck it in the ground, and said, "The sanctuary is built."
Or another translation is, "It is established."
The world-honored one smiled.*

Unlike many of the koans we study, of exchanges between monk and teacher or teacher and teacher dialogue, or the encounter dialogues of Shitou we've heard over the past weeks, this story is about two figures who are beyond our mortal realm: Shakyamuni Buddha, the human form of the succession of seven Buddhas before Buddha, and Indra, king of the gods, who is more like Zeus or one of the Titans in our Greek mythology.
We know him as the creator of Indra's net.
So there are two great world-making spirits at work here.
The Buddha walking with his congregation, his sangha, and his companion who plants a blade of grass that brings forth our phenomenal world in the image of a great net covering the universe.
It's a net in which each multifaceted jeweled intersection, each knot, reflects and embodies all others in an infinitely dynamic, ever-changing framework.
So let's take a moment to consider the story of Buddha's companion who created this net and this grass temple and thus raises a world of practice and devotion.
The sanctuary is built.
It is established.
Some of us have been reading [unclear: "Bill again"] with [unclear: "Shudo Chris"], and reference has often been made to the image of Indra's net.

In my haphazard stumbling, I came across various descriptions and discussions of this story, this net, including a wonderful proposition of its similarity to what we know now as a hologram, a seemingly real object made only of light.
But I found this story of the Buddha the most appropriate for this talk.
*One night at the end of a retreat in Sravasti, one of the followers of Buddha asked him, "Master, what is the ultimate foundation of life and the world?"
Siddhartha Gautama raised his eyes to the sky and contemplated the stars.
Then he smiled as if remembering.

"The ultimate foundation of life and the world is the net of Indra, God of the natural forces that protect and nourish life," he finally said, lowering his eyes to look with affection at his disciple.
"Indra established the foundations of the world in the Tushita heaven.
To do this, he hung over his palace on Mount Sumeru a net of silk threads like a spider web which extends to infinity in all directions.
In each knot of the net, he put a precious gem which reflects in its perfect facets all the other gems that cover the net.

When you approach to look into any one of those gems, you discover that the gems reflected in it reflect in turn each and every one of the other gems of the immense silk fabric, and so on to infinity."*
*"I do not understand, Master," said the disciple, frowning.
"Where are all those gems you're talking about?
I do not see them in this world."*

*"You are one of those gems," Buddha replied, "and every person, every animal, every tree and plant, every insect, every speck of dust that floats up into a sunbeam and down onto a road is a gem on the net of Indra.

Every emotion that you feel and all the feelings that all beings have ever felt even thousands of years ago, and every idea that has crossed the mind of each being since the beginning of time is a gem of Indra's net.
Within you is reflected everything that exists and everything that has ever existed in the universe, and you yourself are reflected in everything that exists.
You are inside each human being, each animal, tree and plant, each speck of dust, each idea or thought, each feeling to infinity.
At every moment the whole world is within you and you are inside everything that exists.
Although in your mind you see yourself*
*as an independent being and you feel separated from the rest of the world, in truth you are part of the common existence of everything that has ever been.

You could never exist by virtue of yourself, by yourself alone, because you exist by virtue of the glorious existence of everything around you.* *A tear appeared in the eye of the disciple, and all the stars in the sky were reflected in it as if in a gem, and Gautama Buddha added, with a look that seemed to caress the soul of the disciple: That is why I say to all of you, take care of the happiness of everything that surrounds you, of all beings, whether you believe that they live or feel or not, because they have their existence also in the depths of your heart.*
What a taproot presentation of Thich Nhat Hanh's interpenetration and the core teaching of codependent origination.
Nothing is separate; each blade of grass is an entire world.
Binding grasses together to build our hut makes a world and contains, as Walt Whitman sings in his great poem Leaves of Grass, a multitude.
When Indra declares the sanctuary is built, he also shows us how little it takes to build that sanctuary, and the vastness of its connectivity.

Dogen in Continuous Practice says: *If you vow to establish a temple, do not be swayed by human concerns, but maintain the strict continuous practice of Buddha Dharma, where the practice is tempered even without a monk's hall*, that is, without a formal traditional structure, *it is a place of enlightenment of old Buddhas.

Where the practice is tempered even without a monk's hall, it is a place of enlightenment of old Buddhas.* Tempered is an interesting word in this context of dealing with limitations, for instance not even having a Buddha hall, because its meaning extends from to strengthen through difficulty, such as tempering a sword or a warrior's courage through battle, to restraining or governing an impulse or to finding a suitable balance.
Dogen continues: *The teaching given outdoors under a tree may be heard afar.

Such a place can be a sacred domain for a long time.* Indeed, he finishes: *The continuous practice of one person will merge with the place of the way of all Buddhas.* Our tempered practice in this time of Zen Zoom is not dependent on a specific place.
Even under a tree, as Dogen says, is old Buddha practice.

The tree under which the Buddha received enlightenment, the Bodhi Tree, is that highly visible sacred domain, but it's also the tree under which Terrell sits above Lake Whatcom, or the room where each of us sits today.
It is our vow to practice that consecrates that space.
We are old Buddha practice, sitting, chanting and bowing together during this session.
The story of Indra's net helps us better appreciate that in one sense it doesn't take much to build a sanctuary.

If we realize, as the introductory comment to this koan says, *as soon as a single mote of dust rises, the whole earth is contained therein.* A few lines later Hong Ji, the compiler of the Book of Serenity, compares that same blade of grass to a sixteen-foot-tall golden Buddha.
What is this blade of grass?
What are the blades of grass that we have constructed our grass hut from?
In the universe of form each particle contains the whole, contains everything, and yet contains nothing.
And that declaration of our place, our intention, is simply to practice the Buddha's teachings here and now in this skin bag, not necessarily to build an edifice or a jade palace or vermilion tower.
In his talk "Respect for Things," Suzuki Roshi tells us: *If we think it is easy to practice because we have a beautiful building, this is a mistake.
Actually it may be quite difficult to practice with a strong spirit in this kind of setting, where we have a handsome Buddha and offer beautiful flowers to decorate our Buddha hall.
We Zen Buddhists have a saying that with a blade of grass we create a golden Buddha which is sixteen feet high.

That is our spirit, so we need to practice respect for things.* He continues: *I don't mean that we should accumulate many leaves of grass just to make a big statue, but until we can see a big Buddha and a small leaf, we need to make much more effort.
How much effort?
I don't know.
Some people may find it quite easy, but for someone like me*, and this is Suzuki Roshi speaking, *for someone like me great effort is needed.

Although seeing a large golden Buddha and a large golden Buddha is easier, when you see a large Buddha and a blade of grass your joy will be something special, so we need to practice respect with great effort.*
Indra shows us how intention can declare a consecrated space.
With that declaration the sanctuary is built.
He also admits that the space will only be temporary, built of grass and perishable.
We could say the same about a jade palace or a granite stupa: what does truly endure?
And when you plant that great blade of grass, it will grow and proliferate.
The speck of dust is raised; the great earth is fully contained therein.
One makes many.
All the universe in William Blake's line, in a grain of sand.
We also know that because of its impermanence, as Wansong comments later in the text, repairs won't be easy.
In a talk on this koan, Zoketsu Fisher said a key reason Everyday Zen doesn't have a physical home is because he didn't want to spend the time raising money to build and take care of a structure.
Shitou tells us, and we know from experience, it will become covered with weeds.
Work will need to be done.
Chop wood, carry water.
Nonetheless we declare our place because we have a need, a desire, to have somewhere to sit with head covered, where all things are at rest, for ourselves and to be with others, our sangha.

Hong Ji's accompanying verse says of the grass: *picking up what comes to hand, he uses it knowingly.* How do we take the elements of our lives, what is in front of us, and build a sanctuary, a grass hut, with expedient means, where we are with what we have?

When we declare our hermitage in our homes, each of us in this sangha becomes, via Zen Zoom, a knot in Indra's net where we sit, and now become part of a virtual sangha we have established with our Zen Zoom mates.
We immediately smile the Buddha smile, and when we sit together in this electronic sanctuary, everything you need is here: in this body, this spot on this earth, in Indra's net.
When we sit here in our own room, wherever that room may be in space and time, nothing is lacking.

I think about all the places I have traveled since beginning practice 10 years ago, and how many times I've sat without a formal zafu, using a folded pillow on the edge of a bed in a strange room in [unclear: "bustled"] in New Zealand or Barcelona, with nothing but a stick of incense, a candle and a tiny brass Buddha.
Or, after a few years into my life with red cedar, a small wooden Buddha amulet that Shuko Edie Norton gifted me, staring at a blank wall.
Or sitting in Loreto or Zihuatanejo, Mexico, with my Dharma brother Robin, staring at a rough stucco wall, with gentle ocean waves, a warm breeze and the squawk of morning birds.
Or in the fo'c'sle of the 62-foot wooden purse seiner, with diesel throbbing, the air saturated with the perfume of bilge water and engine fumes.
And all the pop-up zendos most of us have settled deeply into: Samish, Moon Lake, Asian Center at UBC, and even the Forestry Dharma Hall, consecrated with hours and hours of sweat equity.
All temporary, all impermanent.
Suzuki Roshi tells us that the true ornament of the Buddha Hall is the people who are practicing there.
Each one of us is a beautiful flower, and each one of us is a Buddha leading people, supporting each other in our practice.
He goes on to say:
*We keep studying what will help people practice together.
If you don't forget this point, you will find out how to treat people, how to treat things and how to treat yourself.
This is what we call the Bodhisattva way.
Our practice is to help people, and to help people we found out how to practice in our way in each moment: to stop thinking and to be free from emotional activity when we sit.
This is to rely completely on ourselves, to find absolute refuge in our practice, to find absolute refuge in our practice.*
We can each view our spot, wherever it is, as a kind of Bodhi Mandala, a term traditionally referring to a great pilgrimage temple such as Bodh Gaya, that spot where Buddha attained enlightenment.

But in the Dharma realm of the Buddha pointing to the ground and smiling, when Indra declares the sanctuary is built, it is our lives in this moment, in this place, when we declare our Bodhi Mandala through our practice.

In chapter four of the Vimalakirti Sutra, which came to China in the second century and was in Shitou's deepest marrow, Glorious Light Bodhisattva asked the layman which holy spot, which Bodhi Mandala, he had come from in his recent travels.
Vimalakirti responds not by naming a physical space but by voicing a litany of practices and activities.
He begins with straightforward mind, free from falsehoods, then turns to a recitation of the ten perfections, the four noble truths and a number of other beneficial and expedient actions.
Then he finishes by saying:

*Thus a bodhisattva should convert living beings according to the various modes of perfection, paramitas, and all his acts, including the raising or lowering of a foot, should be interpreted as coming from the sea of learning.*
[unclear: "on dollar"] as well as our true grass hut.
How do we each meet each blade of grass as a Dharma gate, an opportunity to find our Bodhi Mandala, our place?
Recall the line from the Diamond Sutra that awoke the woodcutter who went on to become our sixth patriarch, and Shitou's Dharma grandfather: dwell nowhere and bring forth that mind.
That mind and action are those of a great vehicle bodhisattva, trusting without doubt, living the precepts with joyful ease, living in the world with the Buddha's smile.
In our practice we embody gratitude in our marrow.
Plant your great blade of grass and tend it well.
Remember, you can plant it anywhere.
Attend to ritual and setting, but don't become attached to ritual and setting.
It is all a framework to remind us to pay attention with an open heart to the moment before us, and remember to respect yourself.
Suzuki Roshi, in his talk "Be Kind with Yourself," gives us this blossom:
*If we do not have some warm, big satisfaction in our practice, this is not true practice.*
He tells us to take care of our practice and be very kind with yourself.
Shitou closes his poem with:
*If you want to know the undying person in the hut, don't separate from this skin bag here and now.*
He poses the opportunity to us to be fully here as a choice, if you want.
That choice is each of ours to make: to choose the focus, the body and mind here and now, not on one or the other, but both at the same time, because there is no breaking that bond.
Where do you plant your blade of grass?
How does your practice cultivate and maintain wholesome states for yourself and all you encounter, and the vast earth that sustains us?
Shitou has given us a guidebook.
We have studied the map within the limitations life presents.
How do we find the limitlessness of practice and the continuing joy of sangha life?
After our nap, it will be time to get up, have a cup of tea, till the garden, read a sutra, help our neighbor repair her roof, feed the birds and gather some firewood.
There is no end to what needs to be done.
It is right in front of us.
Thank you for listening to these musings.
May our intentions extend to every being and place with the true merit of the Buddha's way.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
